lesson.title: Half-Life: How Long Until Half Is Gone
lesson.summary: Introduces half-life as the time needed for a quantity to fall to half its starting value, and previews the key question of whether that time stays fixed or shifts as the reaction proceeds.
lesson.body:
Half-life, usually written t1/2, is simply the time required for the concentration of a reactant, or the amount of any decaying quantity, to fall to exactly half of whatever value it started at. It is a concept you have almost certainly met before this course, in contexts like radioactive isotopes used in medicine and archaeology, or the way a drug clears from the bloodstream over the course of a day. Chemistry borrows the same idea and applies it to reactions in general.

It helps to treat half-life, for now, as a purely operational definition: start a clock, watch the concentration, and ask how long it takes to drop by 50 percent. Later in this unit, once the first order integrated rate law has been put to full use, that operational definition gets turned into an exact formula. For the moment, the goal is just to build solid intuition for what "half-life" means and how to use it to track a quantity through repeated halvings.

Here is a fully worked example using successive halvings, the kind of calculation half-life is built for. Suppose a substance in the body is eliminated with a half-life of 4.0 hours, and the initial amount present is 200 mg. After each half-life, exactly half of whatever remains is gone:

t = 0 h: 200 mg
t = 4.0 h (1 half-life): 100 mg
t = 8.0 h (2 half-lives): 50 mg
t = 12.0 h (3 half-lives): 25 mg

The general relationship is amount remaining = initial amount x (1/2)^n, where n is the number of half-lives that have elapsed, n = t / t1/2. Checking the last row directly: 200 mg x (0.5)^3 = 200 mg x 0.125 = 25 mg, matching the step-by-step table exactly.

That worked example raises the single most important open question in this whole topic, and it is the question the next section answers directly: is t1/2 always the same fixed number for a given reaction, no matter how much reactant you started with, or does it shift depending on the starting concentration? The answer turns out to depend entirely on reaction order. For a first order process, the answer is a clean, constant number, which is exactly why half-life became such a famous, widely used concept in the first place, and why the example above could get away with simply stating "a half-life of 4.0 hours" as one fixed number throughout. Not every reaction order behaves so simply, as you already saw a hint of with the second order rate law, and as the next section will make fully explicit.
